en: Sutta Nipāta 1.1 Uragasutta He who subdues the anger that has arisen,
Just as the venom of a snake is neutralized by medicines,
that bhikkhu abandons both this shore and the far shore,
like a snake casting off its old, worn-out skin.
The bhikkhu who has cut off passion without remainder,
having plunged in like a lotus flower amidst a pond,
leaves behind both this shore and the far shore.
Like a snake casting off its worn-out, ancient skin,
he who has cut off craving without remainder has dried up the flowing, swift-moving river.
Thus the bhikkhu abandons both this shore and the far shore,
just as a snake sheds its worn-out, old skin—
whosoever has utterly crushed pride.
Like a great flood sweeping away a very weak reed bridge,
that bhikkhu abandons both this shore and the far shore,
just as a snake sheds its old, worn-out skin.
He who, searching like flowers among udumbara trees, did not find any essence in states of existence—
that bhikkhu leaves behind both this shore and the far shore.
Like a snake casting off its old, worn-out skin,
he whose inner anger has ceased and who has transcended both "it was" and "it will be";
Thus the bhikkhu abandons both this shore and the far shore,
just as a snake sheds its old, worn-out skin.
He whose thoughts have been utterly consumed—
With everything well-ordered within,
that bhikkhu leaves behind both this shore and the far shore,
just as a snake sheds its old, worn-out skin.
He who has not transgressed nor retreated,
who has transcended all this conceptual proliferation—
that bhikkhu leaves behind both this shore and the far shore.
Like a snake casting off its old, worn-out skin,
he who neither retreats nor pursues,
having realized that "all this in the world is false";
Thus the bhikkhu abandons both this shore and the far shore,
like a snake casting off its old, worn-out skin.
He who neither goes forward nor retreats—
"‘All this is false’— thus free from greed,
that bhikkhu abandons both this shore and the far shore,
just as a snake sheds its old, worn-out skin."
He who neither oversteps nor retreats,
being free from passion and knowing that "all this is false," that bhikkhu abandons both this shore and the far shore.
Like a snake casting off its worn-out, ancient skin,
he who neither retreats nor pursues,
being free from hatred, knows: "All this is false."
Thus the bhikkhu abandons both this shore and the far shore,
just as a snake sheds its old, worn-out skin;
he who neither goes forward nor retreats.
"Everything is false"— thus free from delusion,
that bhikkhu leaves behind both this shore and the far shore,
like a snake casting off its old, worn-out skin.
He in whom no underlying tendencies remain,
and whose unwholesome roots have been utterly uprooted—
that bhikkhu abandons both this shore and the far shore.
Like a snake casting off its old, worn-out skin—
therein no afflictions arise for him who has no conditions for returning to the near shore.
Thus the bhikkhu abandons both this shore and the far shore,
just as a snake sheds its old, worn-out skin;
he for whom no undergrowth of the forest exists.
A cause for bondage and for existence;
such a bhikkhu abandons both this shore and the far shore,
just as a snake sheds its old, worn-out skin.
He who, having abandoned the five hindrances,
is free from distress, has crossed beyond doubt, and is without taints—
that bhikkhu leaves behind both this shore and the far shore.
Like a snake sheds its worn-out skin, so it is with the old.
Thus ends the first discourse, the Uragasutta.
